reel.title: 3 missiles at Riyadh, a threat to Saudi ports | Why oil still fell
reel.hook: 3 MISSILES AT RIYADH. HOUTHIS THREATEN [SAUDI PORTS]
reel.topic: Saudi-Houthi escalation of 19-21 Nov and what it means for oil. Thursday: a Houthi attack damaged the Public Investment Fund tower in Riyadh (Saudi statement via Al Jazeera/Reuters). Friday: the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians away from Yemen's Hodeidah port, then said it destroyed 'operational capabilities at the port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles' (AFP, Reuters); Yemen's information minister said the port 'remains fully operational' (Reuters). Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree: 'Jeddah port and all ports of the Saudi enemy on the Red Sea coast will be a target' (via Middle East Eye), workers should 'evacuate them immediately and stay away', shipping companies should pull their ships out, airlines should avoid Saudi airspace (via Reuters). Early Saturday: the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles fired towards Riyadh (Reuters, AFP, Arab News); the Houthis said they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia. Why it matters for oil: Saudi Arabia's 1,200 km East-West pipeline ends at Yanbu on the Red Sea and has a maximum capacity of about 7 million barrels a day (Al Jazeera, 17 Sep; OilPrice.com). The market: oil fell for a third week; Reuters put it down to strong Middle East export flows (BNP Paribas's Aldo Spanjer) and the stock selloff (Saxo). The catch: Iran's Guards claim 30+ ships hit mines this month, announced 'almost daily since mid-October'; analysts told The National they see almost no evidence of mine damage; UOB (via Reuters) counts roughly one tanker incident a day in November and says it adds a risk premium. Next: OPEC+ ministers meet on 29 Nov to decide 2027 output policy.
